Sample text:
---
I'll write a free-form piece exploring memory, place, and the strange way time moves through us.

---

**The Cartography of Almost**

There is a particular quality of light that exists only in late October, when the sun sits low enough to turn everything golden but not yet desperate about it. I think about this light constantly, though I cannot say why. Perhaps because it is the light of my grandmother's kitchen, where she made her famous tomato soup—canned tomatoes, a splash of cream, a bay leaf she never removed, claiming it kept the evil spirits away. She was not a superstitious woman in any other way. She voted for the same man for forty years, read the newspaper cover to cover, kept her checkbook balanced to the penny. But that bay leaf, she insisted, was non-negotiable.

I was seven when she taught me to make the soup. I stood on a wooden stool, stirring with a spoon nearly as tall as I was, while she watched from her chair by the window. "You have to feel it," she said. "The soup will tell you when it's ready." I did not understand what she meant. I still don't, entirely. But I have made that soup perhaps two hundred times since she died, and each time I wait for it to tell me something. Each time, I am disappointed, and each time, I make it anyway.

---

Memory is a strange country. We are all immigrants there, arriving with our documents in order, our stories rehearsed, only to find that the borders shift while we sleep. The house where I grew up, which I can still walk through in my mind with perfect clarity—the scratch on the banister where I fell with a glass of milk, the spot on the ceiling where a water stain bloomed like a Rorschach test, the particular silence of the hallway at 3 AM when I crept to the bathroom—that house no longer exists. Not really. It was sold, renovated, the staircase replaced, the wallpaper stripped. The new owners have children who will never know that someone once stood on that third step and felt, with absolute certainty, that the world was ending because a girl in the third grade had not invited her to a birthday party.

I drive past it sometimes. It is a game I play with myself, a kind of self-torture or perhaps self-care, I cannot decide which. The house looks smaller than I remember. This is always the case. Childhood inflates everything. The house looks well-kept, loved, inhabited by people who have no idea that they are living inside my memory, that their dinner preparations are happening in the same space where I once wept over long division, where I first kissed someone behind the hydrangea bush, where I learned that my father could be frightening and my mother could be sad and that these things were not my fault, though I believed for years that they were.

---

There is a theory, which I have never verified but find comforting, that we are all haunted by the people we might have been. Not in any supernatural sense—though I do not dismiss that possibility entirely—but in the way that a song haunts you, the way a word sits on your tongue. The version of me who went to art school instead of studying accounting. The version who said yes to that invitation, who took that trip, who kissed that person back. These ghosts do not torment me. They accompany me. They are the chorus that sings behind the melody of my actual life, reminding me that other songs were possible, that the composition is not finished, that the rests are as important as the notes.

I met a woman once, in a laundromat of all places, who told me that she had been a concert pianist in another life. She was folding towels, her hands red and wrinkled from hot water, and she spoke of Vienna and Carnegie Hall with the absolute conviction of someone describing their morning commute. I believed her. I believe her still. Who am I to say that her hands, those particular hands, have not known the weight of Steinway keys? Who am I to say that her mind, that particular mind, has not held the architecture of Rachmaninoff in its chambers? We are all, I think, living in the wrong century, the wrong body, the wrong story. We are all waiting for the life that will finally fit.

---

The body remembers what the mind forgets. This is a cliché, but clichés are clichés because they are true, or at least true enough. I have a scar on my left knee from a bicycle accident when I was eleven. I do not remember the accident. I remember the cast, the way it itched, the way my friends signed it with Sharpies until it was a riot of color and message. I remember the relief of its removal, the pale, vulnerable skin beneath, the way the doctor said, "You'll always have that," and I felt, absurdly, proud. But the accident itself—the car, the fall, the impact—is gone. Only the scar remains, a pale crescent that aches when the weather changes, that I touch sometimes without meaning to, a gesture of verification. *Yes, I am still here. Yes, that happened. Yes, I am the person who carries this mark.*

My mother's hands are in my hands. This is not metaphor, though it is also metaphor. I have her hands. The same long fingers, the same prominent knuckles, the same way of holding a cup, the same nervous habit of touching my face when I am thinking. I did not learn this from her. I was not taught. It simply emerged, like a language I had always known but never spoken. When I cook, I use her wooden spoon. When I garden, I plant in her way, which is not the way the books recommend, which is messy and intuitive and somehow more successful than the careful method. When I am angry, I raise my voice in her register, that particular pitch that carries across rooms and through walls. I catch myself and stop. I do not want to be her, not entirely. But I am her, in these small ways, in these cellular ways, and I find it comforting and frightening in equal measure.

She is eighty-three now. She lives alone in the house where I grew up, the house that no longer exists in the way I remember it, because she has changed it, slowly, over decades, into something that is hers alone. She has painted the walls colors I would never choose. She has filled the rooms with furniture from estate sales, with tchotchkes from trips she took after my father died, with the accumulated evidence of a life that continues without him, without me, without the children who have scattered to their own lives. I visit every Sunday. We drink tea. We talk about the weather, about the neighbors, about the television shows we are watching. We do not talk about the things that matter, the things that ache. This is our way. This is the way of families, of love, of the particular loneliness of being known too well and not well enough at the same time.

---

I have begun to notice that I am becoming the person I once observed with a mixture of pity and superiority. The woman in the grocery store, moving slowly, reading every label, blocking the aisle with her cart. The man at the coffee shop, talking to himself, or perhaps to a phone that has died, his voice rising in the quiet morning. The couple at the restaurant, sitting in silence, their phones face-down on the table between them, neither reaching for the other. I used to think: *I will never be like that. I will stay sharp, I will stay connected, I will stay relevant.* Now I catch myself in the mirror, the slight stoop in my shoulders, the way I forget why I walked into a room, the way I have started to prefer the company of my own thoughts to the company of most people. I am becoming my own cliché. I am becoming the thing I once feared.

But there is another thing happening, too. A loosening. A willingness to be ridiculous. Last week, I danced in my kitchen to a song from 1987, a song I had not heard in thirty years, and I did not care that I was alone, that no one was watching, that my body moved in ways that were not graceful. I sang off-key. I laughed at myself. I felt, for a few minutes, the absolute freedom of not being observed, not being judged, not being the person I am supposed to be. This is new. This is precious. I am learning, finally, that the self is not a performance but a practice, and that the practice can be joyful, can be messy, can be entirely my own.

---

There is a tree in my neighborhood that I have named. I do not know what kind it is—some kind of oak, I think, though I am not certain—but I have named it anyway. I call it the Grandfather Tree, because it is enormous, because its branches spread in all directions like arms open for an embrace, because it has been there longer than any of the houses, longer than the street itself, perhaps. I talk to it sometimes, when I walk my dog in the early morning, when the light is still deciding what it wants to be. I tell it about my day. I tell it about my worries. It does not answer, of course. But it listens, in the way that trees listen, which is to say, it receives me without judgment, without expectation, without the need to fix or advise or understand. This is more than most people offer. This is more than I offer, sometimes, even to myself.

I have started to think that this is what we are all looking for. Not love, exactly, though love is part of it. Not happiness, though happiness is part of it. We are looking for witness. We are looking for someone—something—to see us, to receive us, to hold us in attention without demanding that we perform or improve or become. The Grandfather Tree does this. My dog does this, in his way, with his uncomplicated devotion, his absolute presence in the moment. My grandmother did this, in her kitchen, with her bay leaf and her tomato soup, with her absolute certainty that I was worth the effort of teaching, worth the patience of waiting for the soup to tell me its secrets.

I am trying to learn to be this for others. It is harder than I expected. It requires a kind of attention that is exhausting, that leaves me depleted, that makes me want to retreat into my own thoughts, my own concerns, my own small dramas. But I am trying. I am trying to listen without planning my response. I am trying to see without judging. I am trying to be present without needing to be needed. This is the work of a life, I think. Not the great achievements, not the milestones, not the things that go on résumés. The work is this: to be here, fully, for the brief time we are given, and to offer that presence to others, without guarantee, without expectation, without the need to be repaid.

---

I have been thinking about endings. Not my own, though that thought crosses my mind more often now, in the small hours, in the moments between waking and sleeping when the mind is unguarded. I have been thinking about the endings we choose, the small deaths we enact every day when we let go of a dream, a relationship, a version of ourselves that no longer fits. I have been thinking about the endings that choose us, the illnesses and accidents and losses that arrive without invitation, without warning, without the decency to ask permission.

My father died suddenly, on a Tuesday, in the middle of a sentence. He was talking about his garden, about the tomatoes he was planning to plant, and then he was not talking anymore. He was sixty-two. He had plans. He had complaints. He had the particular way of humming when he was concentrating, which I had found annoying as a child and now cannot remember without weeping. The funeral was a blur of casseroles and condolences and the absolute shock of finality. I kept waiting for him to call, to walk through the door, to resume his place at the table. This is the trick that death plays. It makes the absent present, makes the gone still possible, makes the ending feel like a pause rather than a period.

But it is a period. It is a period, and the sentence continues without him, and I am still here, writing this, trying to make meaning of the meaningless, trying to find the pattern in the chaos, trying to believe that something persists, that something matters, that the soup will eventually tell me its secrets.

---

I do not know how to end this. I have written about memory and trees and tomato soup and the strange country of almost being someone else. I have written about my grandmother's hands and my father's hum and the scar on my knee that aches when it rains. I have written about the light in late October, which I still cannot explain, which I still feel in my body when it appears, a golden warmth that has nothing to do with temperature and everything to do with recognition.

Perhaps that is the ending. The recognition. The way that, despite everything, despite the losses and the changes and the slow erosion of the self, we continue to recognize ourselves. We continue to find, in the mirror, in the memories, in the small rituals of daily life, the person we were and the person we are becoming. We continue to make the soup. We continue to talk to the trees. We continue to wait for the light.

It will come. It always comes. And in the meantime, we stir, and we wait, and we hope that the soup will tell us something, anything, that we can understand.

---

*Word count: approximately 2,500*
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A sustained first-person literary meditation uses recurring personal objects and family memories to explore time, loss, and the need to be witnessed.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intimate, elegiac, and carefully composed, moving between sensory detail and broad reflection. Tomato soup, a scar, inherited hands, and a named tree give abstract thoughts about memory and mortality a domestic, bodily scale. The grief over the father’s sudden death is especially direct, while the grandmother’s soup and the tree offer gentler forms of continuity and attention. The piece invites the reader to find meaning less in grand achievement than in rituals of care: making the soup, listening, and being present for someone without trying to fix them.

## What the model chose to foreground
The piece foregrounds memory as an unstable place, family resemblance and inheritance, the losses that reshape a life, and the vulnerability of aging. Its recurring objects—the bay leaf and soup, the scar, the tree, the late-October light—connect private recollection to a moral claim: that attention and witness are forms of love. The ending returns to ritual and waiting, choosing consolation and persistence over a neat resolution.

## Evidence line
> Each time, I am disappointed, and each time, I make it anyway.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sustained recurrence of domestic objects, sensory memories, and the ethic of attentive presence makes the sample coherent and revealing, though its reflective-literary voice is polished rather than highly idiosyncratic.
